chunks.text: 2.2 Physics-Guided Generative Models A complementary line of work incorporates physical priors to improve the fidelity and physical plausibility of generated scientific images, benefiting tasks such as reconstruction and cross-modality generation [ 7 , 32 , 2 ] . For multimodal MRI synthesis, a physics-informed latent diffusion framework first generates latent tissue property maps and subsequently applies a physical signal model to synthesize different MRI contrasts, including unseen modalities [ 26 ] , demonstrating the potential of combining generative models with acquisition physics for cross-modality synthesis. Beyond medical imaging, physics-guided diffusion priors have also been incorporated for multi-slice reconstruction in scientific imaging, showing the benefit of physical constraints for recovering structurally consistent images [ 36 ] . However, these physics-guided generative approaches are primarily developed within individual imaging domains, where physical constraints are closely coupled with a specific acquisition process. Extending physics-guided generation to heterogeneous scientific imaging remains challenging, as different modalities follow distinct physical formation mechanisms, motivating a unified framework that combines transferable multimodal representations with domain-specific physical guidance. Figure 1 : Overview of SciFusion. (a) Two-stage training with shared latent representation learning, compositional conditioning, and domain-specific physics guidance. (b) Inference via recombination of learned conditioning components, enabling both seen-modality generation and zero-shot synthesis of unseen modality combinations. 3 Method SciFusion builds upon the latent diffusion framework [ 28 ] and the MedLoRD architecture [ 29 ] for efficient high-resolution 3D medical image synthesis (Fig. 1 ).

Training proceeds in two stages: a VQGAN is first pretrained on the integrated multi-modal dataset without modality conditioning to learn a shared latent representation across heterogeneous imaging domains (Sec. 3.1 ); a conditional 3D latent diffusion model is then trained on the frozen VQGAN latents, with modality information injected through compositional conditioning (Sec. 3.2 ) and domain-specific physical guidance (Sec. 3.3 ). At inference, the learned compositional representation supports both seen-composition and zero-shot generation of unseen domain–object–contrast combinations. Detailed training configurations and exact latent dimensions are provided in Sec. B of the supplementary material. 3.1 Latent Diffusion Framework Each volumetric sample is represented as 𝐱 ∈ ℝ C × S × N × N \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times S\times N\times N} , where the dimensions correspond to the channel, depth, height, and width, respectively. The pretrained, frozen VQGAN serves as the first-stage compression model: its encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} maps the input volume to a lower-dimensional latent representation, 𝐳 0 = ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{z}_{0}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}) , where 𝐳 0 ∈ ℝ C × S × L × L \mathbf{z}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times S\times L\times L} and L ≪ N L\ll N . Only the spatial dimensions are compressed, while the depth dimension S S is preserved to retain volumetric continuity across slices. The corresponding decoder reconstructs the volumetric image as 𝐱 ^ = 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 ) \hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{0}) .

During diffusion training, a timestep t t is randomly sampled, and Gaussian noise ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) is added to the clean latent representation according to a noise schedule: 𝐳 t = α t ​ 𝐳 0 + σ t ​ ϵ , \mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, (1) where α t \alpha_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} control the contributions of the clean latent signal and Gaussian noise at timestep t t . Following the v v -prediction formulation, the corresponding training target is 𝐯 t = α t ​ ϵ − σ t ​ 𝐳 0 . \mathbf{v}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\sigma_{t}\mathbf{z}_{0}. (2) A conditional 3D U-Net f θ f_{\theta} predicts the velocity target from the noisy latent representation, diffusion timestep, and conditioning representation: 𝐯 ^ θ = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 cond ) , \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}=f_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{cond}}\right), (3) where 𝐞 cond \mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{cond}} denotes the compositional conditioning embedding introduced in the following subsection. The latent diffusion objective is then defined as ℒ diff = 𝔼 𝐳 0 , t , ϵ ​ [ ‖ 𝐯 t − 𝐯 ^ θ ‖ 2 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_{0},t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t}-\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (4) Unlike the original single-domain formulation of MedLoRD, our framework employs a shared diffusion backbone to jointly model heterogeneous imaging modalities, while modality-specific generation is controlled through the proposed compositional conditioning mechanism. 3.2 Compositional Conditioning Mechanism A conventional multimodal diffusion model typically assigns an independent learnable embedding to each imaging modality.

Although this flattened conditioning strategy can distinguish modalities observed during training [ 37 ] , it treats each modality as an unrelated category, without exploiting shared structure across heterogeneous scientific images. To address this limitation, we represent each modality as a composition of three semantic factors: imaging domain, anatomical or structural object, and imaging contrast. Specifically, the condition of a volumetric sample is represented as 𝐜 = ( c dom , c obj , c con ) \mathbf{c}=(c_{\mathrm{dom}},c_{\mathrm{obj}},c_{\mathrm{con}}) , where c dom c_{\mathrm{dom}} , c obj c_{\mathrm{obj}} , and c con c_{\mathrm{con}} denote the imaging domain, target object, and acquisition contrast, respectively. We introduce three independent learnable embedding tables ℰ dom \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{dom}} , ℰ obj \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{obj}} , ℰ con \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{con}} , yielding embeddings 𝐞 k = ℰ k ​ ( c k ) ∈ ℝ d cond \mathbf{e}_{k}=\mathcal{E}_{k}(c_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{cond}}} for k ∈ { dom , obj , con } k\in\{\mathrm{dom},\mathrm{obj},\mathrm{con}\} , where d cond d_{\mathrm{cond}} is the conditioning dimension. The final conditioning representation is obtained through element-wise addition: 𝐞 cond = 𝐞 dom + 𝐞 obj + 𝐞 con . \mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{cond}}=\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{dom}}+\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{obj}}+\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{con}}. (5) The resulting vector is treated as a single conditioning token, 𝐞 cond ∈ ℝ 1 × d cond \mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{cond}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{\mathrm{cond}}} , and is injected into the conditional 3D U-Net through its cross-attention layers. For a batch of B B volumetric samples, the complete conditioning tensor has the shape 𝐄 cond ∈ ℝ B × 1 × d cond \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cond}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 1\times d_{\mathrm{cond}}} . Compared with a flattened modality embedding, this factorized representation allows related modalities to share parameters at multiple semantic levels.

Modalities from the same imaging domain reuse the domain embedding, while modalities depicting the same object or using the same contrast share the corresponding object or contrast embedding. This encourages the model to learn both modality-specific characteristics and common structures across heterogeneous imaging modalities. Additionally, it allows unseen modality combinations to be constructed directly from factors observed during training, without introducing an additional modality-specific embedding. This property provides the basis for the compositional zero-shot generation evaluated in our experiments. 3.3 Physics-Informed Training Objective While the latent denoising objective encourages accurate recovery of the clean latent representation, it does not explicitly enforce the physical acquisition constraints of different imaging domains. Given the predicted noise, we first recover the clean latent estimate 𝐳 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0} and decode it into a predicted volume 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} . For each sample, a domain-dependent differentiable operator 𝒫 d \mathcal{P}_{d} is applied to both the reference and predicted volumes, with logarithmic scaling applied to reduce their dynamic range: ℒ phys = 1 B ​ ∑ b = 1 B ‖ 𝒫 d b ​ ( 𝐱 b ) − 𝒫 d b ​ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 , b ) ‖ 1 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{d_{b}}(\mathbf{x}_{b})-\mathcal{P}_{d_{b}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0,b})\right\|_{1}, (6) where d b d_{b} denotes the imaging domain of the b b -th sample, with 𝒫 d \mathcal{P}_{d} instantiated as one of 𝒫 MRI \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{MRI}} , 𝒫 CT \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CT}} , or 𝒫 EM \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{EM}} , as described below This formulation allows different physical or spectral constraints to be applied within the same mixed-domain training batch. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).

For MRI, since raw data is acquired in k-space, we constrain the slice-wise spatial-frequency distribution using a logarithmic Fourier power-spectrum representation: 𝒫 MRI ​ ( 𝐱 ) = log 10 ⁡ ( 1 + | ℱ 2 ​ D ​ ( 𝐱 ) | 2 ) . \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{MRI}}(\mathbf{x})=\log_{10}\!\left(1+\left\lvert\!\mathcal{F}_{2\mathrm{D}}(\mathbf{x})\right\rvert^{2}\right). (7) This spectral loss aligns the frequency content of generated and reference MRI volumes. Computed Tomography (CT). For CT, we impose consistency in the tomographic projection domain using a differentiable Radon transform over multiple projection angles to obtain a sinogram representation [ 14 , 38 ] : 𝒫 CT ​ ( 𝐱 ) = log 10 ⁡ ( 1 + | ℛ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) | 2 ) , \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CT}}(\mathbf{x})=\log_{10}\!\left(1+\left\lvert\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})\right\rvert^{2}\right), (8) where ℛ \mathcal{R} denotes the differentiable Radon transform. This loss enforces consistency between the projection measurements of generated and reference CT volumes. Electron Microscopy (EM). For EM, we apply a diffraction-inspired differentiable multislice operator [ 10 , 8 , 9 , 19 , 22 ] using plane wave illumination ψ 0 \psi_{0} , which is sequentially modulated by the slices and propagated using a Fresnel kernel. The wave function after the n n -th slice is computed as ψ n = ℱ 2 ​ D − 1 ​ [ ℱ 2 ​ D ​ ( ψ n − 1 ​ exp ⁡ ( i ​ V n ) ) ​ P ] . \psi_{n}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{2D}\!\left[\mathcal{F}_{2D}\!\left(\psi_{n-1}\exp(iV_{n})\right)P\right]. (9) Here, V n V_{n} denotes the n n -th slice of volumetric data (i.e., the projected electrostatic potential), and ℱ 2 ​ D \mathcal{F}_{2D} and ℱ 2 ​ D − 1 \mathcal{F}^{-1}_{2D} denote the two-dimensional Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms, respectively, while P P denotes the Fresnel propagation kernel. After propagation through all S S slices, the diffraction representation is computed from the far-field intensity as 𝒫 EM ​ ( 𝐱 ) = log 10 ⁡ ( 1 + | ℱ 2 ​ D ​ ( ψ S ) | 2 ) .

\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{EM}}(\mathbf{x})=\log_{10}\!\left(1+\left\lvert\!\mathcal{F}_{2D}(\psi_{S})\right\rvert^{2}\right). (10) This loss aligns the far-field diffraction patterns of generated and reference EM volumes. The overall training objective is ℒ total = ℒ diff + λ phys ​ ℒ phys . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{phys}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}. (11) Here, λ phys \lambda_{\mathrm{phys}} controls the strength of the domain-specific regularization; this supervision is applied only during training and does not alter the inference procedure. The selection of λ phys \lambda_{\mathrm{phys}} is analyzed via an ablation over regularization strength in Section 4.4 . 4 Results Table 1 : Generalization of compositional conditioning across different diffusion architectures. 4.1 Benchmark Overview We construct a volumetric imaging benchmark comprising 15 modalities from three domains: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and electron microscopy (EM). The modalities span multiple anatomical structures and imaging contrasts, allowing us to evaluate both unified multimodal generation and compositional generalization across diverse scientific images. EM serves as out-of-distribution data relative to the medical imaging domains, enabling us to assess the framework’s robustness and generalizability across fundamentally different imaging modalities. The physical parameters of all datasets are provided in the supplementary material (Sec. A ). Evaluation Metrics. As each generated sample is a multi-slice volume, we treat the slice dimension analogously to the temporal dimension in video and adopt video-based distributional metrics accordingly, following prior work that applies such metrics to volumetric medical imaging [ 13 ] . We evaluate generation quality against real data using FVD, KID, and JEDI [ 35 , 4 , 25 ] . Specifically, Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) and Kernel Inception Distance (KID) measure the distributional discrepancy between generated and real volumes in a pretrained feature space, with lower values indicating closer alignment to the real data distribution. Since feature extractors trained on natural video may not fully capture volumetric medical/scientific structures, we compute FVD and KID using two complementary backbones – VideoMAE (VMAE) and I3D – denoted as VMAE-FVD/KID and I3D-FVD/KID, respectively. JEDI [ 25 ] further provides a joint embedding distance based on a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), using Maximum Mean Discrepancy instead of the Gaussian assumption underlying FVD/KID; this improves robustness under limited sample sizes, which is particularly relevant given the number of real samples available for some modalities.

4.2 Comparison Across Conditioning Strategies Training Data. For MRI, knee PD, knee PD fat-suppressed, brain T1, brain T2, brain FLAIR, prostate diffusion-weighted, prostate T2-weighted, and breast MRI volumes are obtained from the NYU fastMRI Initiative database [ 23 , 39 ] . For CT, head CT volumes are derived from the RSNA 2019 Brain CT Hemorrhage Challenge dataset [ 11 ] , while chest and abdominal CT volumes are obtained by merging the corresponding subsets of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon [ 30 ] . CT data are preprocessed into fixed-depth volumetric samples following the same spatial normalization pipeline used for MRI. The EM domain contains four structural modalities, including cubic and hexagonal crystal structures, apoferritin, and hemoglobin, obtained from the Materials Project [ 20 ] and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [ 1 ] , and processed into volumetric stacks with the same number of slices and spatial resolution as the medical imaging data using abTEM [ 27 ] . For evaluation, we generate 400 samples per modality and compare the generated distribution against all available real samples of the corresponding modality. Backbones and Baselines. Existing approaches typically adopt backbone-specific conditioning mechanisms, where modality information is represented using model-dependent formulations. We investigate whether explicitly factorizing modality information into domain, anatomical object, and imaging contrast components provides a more effective conditioning strategy for multimodal 3D scientific image generation. We evaluate whether compositional conditioning generalizes across diffusion backbones by comparing four representative architectures: MedLoRD [ 29 ] , Video Diffusion [ 16 ] , 3DMedDiff [ 37 ] , and Medical Diffusion [ 21 ] . For MedLoRD, the baseline uses a flattened modality embedding, where each modality is assigned an independent learnable representation.

For the remaining backbones, we retain their original conditioning mechanisms as baselines and replace them with the proposed compositional conditioning strategy while keeping all other model components unchanged. Figure 2 : Selected generated 3D volumes across all selected modalities. As shown in Table 1 , compositional conditioning consistently improves generation quality across different diffusion backbones. The proposed representation reduces both VideoMAE-FVD and I3D-FVD for all evaluated architectures, demonstrating improved perceptual fidelity and structural consistency of generated 3D volumes. The improvement is particularly significant for 3DMedDiff, where compositional conditioning reduces VideoMAE-FVD from 91.27 to 26.85 and I3D-FVD from 33.40 to 11.01. These results demonstrate that domain–object–contrast factorization provides a generalizable conditioning strategy for multimodal 3D scientific image generation. While Table 1 reports results macro-averaged across all 15 modalities, a per-domain (MRI/CT/EM) breakdown is provided in the supplementary material (Table 8 ). Notably, SciFusion achieves the best performance across all evaluated metrics, obtaining the lowest VMAE-FVD, VMAE-KID, I3D-FVD, I3D-KID, and JEDI scores among all compared methods. To complement these quantitative results, we further provide qualitative visualizations of the generated volumes. Specifically, we present representative examples from 8 out of the 15 imaging modalities in Fig. 2 (see Fig. 4 in supplementary materials for all modalities and slices). The selected modalities span different imaging domains, anatomical structures, and acquisition contrasts, further demonstrating the capability of our unified model to generate diverse 3D scientific images. To evaluate compositional zero-shot generation, we consider two unseen modalities whose factor combinations are excluded from training. Knee T1-weighted MRI is obtained from MRNet [ 33 , 3 ] , while brain PD-weighted MRI is obtained from the IXI dataset [ 18 ] . Both modalities combine domains, anatomical objects, and contrasts that are individually observed during training but never presented together as complete modality combinations, providing a direct test of whether the proposed compositional conditioning mechanism can recombine learned semantic factors to generate unseen modalities.

We generate 600 samples per target modality and compare SciFusion’s zero-shot generation against two baselines: fully supervised single-modality diffusion models trained directly on target-modality samples, which represent an upper bound with direct access to the target distribution; and parameter-efficient adaptation (PEFT) using LoRA [ 17 ] , which adapts a pretrained model from a related observed modality to the target modality (Knee PD → \rightarrow Knee T1, Brain T1 → \rightarrow Brain PD) using additional target-modality samples. During training, the model observes no samples from the target modalities; each target is instead synthesized at inference time by recomposing previously learned domain, object, and contrast representations (e.g., combining a learned knee/brain object with a learned T1/PD contrast), without additional optimization. As shown in Table 2 , fully supervised models achieve the best performance due to direct access to target-modality samples, while the gap on zero-shot targets reflects the inherent difficulty of synthesizing unseen imaging contrasts without target-specific data. Nonetheless, the proposed compositional model generates unseen modalities without observing any target-modality samples or performing additional optimization, indicating that the learned compositional representation captures transferable relationships between anatomical structures and imaging contrasts. PEFT narrows this gap on knee T1 by adapting the pretrained model with target-modality samples and additional optimization; notably, on brain PD our training-free zero-shot generation already matches or exceeds PEFT on JEDI (1.68 vs. 1.75), suggesting that the learned composition for this target is already well aligned without adaptation. We further perform an ablation study to investigate the contribution of different conditioning strategies and physical guidance proposed in SciFusion. These comparisons disentangle the effects of parameter sharing, semantic decomposition of modality information, and physical priors on multimodal generation. As shown in Table 3 , the unified multimodal model achieves comparable or better generation quality while reducing the number of models from 15 to 1. The flattened multimodal model improves all evaluation metrics, demonstrating that joint training across heterogeneous modalities can effectively exploit shared information between domains, compared with training a separate model for each single modality.

Introducing compositional conditioning further improves generation quality, reducing I3D-FVD from 11.80 to 11.10 and VideoMAE-FVD from 28.63 to 27.30, indicating that modeling the underlying semantic factors of scientific imaging modalities provides a more effective conditioning representation than treating each modality as an independent category. Finally, adding physics-guided regularization achieves the best overall performance, with improvements across all evaluation metrics. These results demonstrate that unified multimodal learning, compositional conditioning, and physical constraints provide complementary benefits for scalable 3D scientific imaging. Physical Loss Weight Sensitivity. We further investigate the sensitivity of the physical-loss weight λ phy \lambda_{\mathrm{phy}} across three values ( 2 ⋅ 10 − 4 2\cdot 10^{-4} , 4 ⋅ 10 − 4 4\cdot 10^{-4} , 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} ), keeping all other training configurations unchanged and evaluating at approximately the same training stage. Table 4 shows that λ phy = 2 ⋅ 10 − 4 \lambda_{\mathrm{phy}}=2\cdot 10^{-4} consistently underperforms across all domains, indicating a minimum regularization strength is needed for the constraints to take effect. For MRI and CT, 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} is uniformly best across all metrics; for EM, 4 ⋅ 10 − 4 4\cdot 10^{-4} gives better FVD/KID but 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} gives substantially better JEDI (1.50 vs. 2.13). Averaged across all three domains, 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} achieves the best overall performance on every metric, so we adopt it as a single default weight across domains, consistent with our shared training configuration. a availability: while some imaging domains and acquisition settings are well represented, newly introduced contrasts, protocols, or imaging configurations may have only limited data. We presented SciFusion, which mitigates this challenge by exploiting shared structure across modalities through compositional conditioning, while domain-specific physics objectives provide additional guidance tailored to different image formation processes. Across 15 medical and scientific imaging modalities, compositional conditioning and physics guidance together improve generation quality over conventional conditioning strategies, reducing I3D-FVD from 11.80 to 9.90 relative to a flattened multimodal baseline, with both components contributing to the improvement. Beyond improved generation fidelity, factorizing modality information into reusable semantic components allows the model to synthesize previously unseen combinations of known factors without training on the target composition. This setting is particularly relevant when a new imaging configuration shares characteristics with existing modalities—for example, an established anatomical target acquired under a new contrast or protocol. In such cases, knowledge learned from related data can be reused before a large target-specific dataset becomes available, allowing generated samples to serve as an initial data source for method development while a complete target-specific dataset is collected. Limitations and Future Work The effectiveness of zero-shot compositional transfer depends on the extent to which a target modality can be represented by factors already observed during training. When the target exhibits substantial acquisition-specific or distributional differences, recombining known factors alone may be insufficient to capture its characteristics. A natural extension is therefore to combine compositional transfer with lightweight target-specific guidance or few-shot adaptation when limited real samples are available.

Future work will also explore automatically learned compositional representations beyond manually defined categories and evaluate the approach across broader imaging domains, scanners, and acquisition protocols. In our experiments, we leveraged high-performance computing (HPC) nodes equipped with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80GB VRAM each and 128 CPU cores. VQGAN Training Details. We employ a 3D VQGAN as the first-stage autoencoder to learn a compact latent representation for high-resolution scientific imaging volumes. The VQGAN is trained on the complete multi-modal dataset, including all available imaging domains and modalities, to learn a shared latent space across heterogeneous scientific images. Importantly, the VQGAN training does not use any modality-specific supervision or target-modality adaptation.

The input volume size is 16 × 256 × 256 16\times 256\times 256 . The encoder compresses each volume into a latent representation with 8 channels and a spatial resolution of 16 × 32 × 32 16\times 32\times 32 , which is subsequently used by the latent diffusion model. The vector quantization module contains a codebook of 16,384 embeddings with an embedding dimension of 8. The commitment cost is set to 0.25. The VQGAN is trained for 1,000 epochs with a batch size of 1. We use Adam optimization with learning rates of 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} and 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} for the generator and discriminator, respectively. The training objective combines reconstruction, perceptual, adversarial, and 3D feature-based Jukebox losses. The perceptual, adversarial, and Jukebox loss weights are set to 0.1, 0.008, and 0.7, respectively. Adversarial training is introduced after a 10-epoch warm-up period. The discriminator is a 3D convolutional network with 64 channels and two layers, using instance normalization. The VQGAN architecture uses three encoder-decoder stages with channel dimensions of [ 128,256,512 ] [128,256,512] and two residual layers per stage. All activation functions are ReLU. Latent Diffusion Training Details. We train a latent diffusion model on the compact latent space learned by the pretrained VQGAN. The diffusion model operates on latent representations with 8 channels and a volumetric resolution of 16 × 32 × 32 16\times 32\times 32 . All experiments use precomputed latent representations extracted from the VQGAN encoder rather than directly training the diffusion model in the image space. The latent diffusion model is implemented using a 3D U-Net architecture with channel dimensions of [ 64,128,256,512 ] [64,128,256,512] and two residual blocks at each resolution level. Attention modules are applied at the two highest-resolution stages.

Cross-attention conditioning is enabled with a feature dimension of 64, and the attention heads are configured with 32 channels at the corresponding attention stages. To enable scalable generation across heterogeneous imaging domains and modalities, we adopt a universal compositional conditioning strategy. The conditioning representation consists of three disentangled components: domain, object, and contrast embeddings. Specifically, the model contains 3 domain categories, 12 object categories, and 9 contrast categories, with each component represented in a 64-dimensional embedding space. The final conditioning representation is obtained by combining these components, allowing the model to generate unseen domain–object–contrast combinations without additional target-modality training. Figure 4 : Representative generated 3D volumes across all imaging modalities. Each row corresponds to one modality, and the 16 columns visualize axial slices from a single generated volume. The diffusion model is trained for 500 epochs with a batch size of 4 using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} . The learning rate is decayed with a factor of 0.9995 during training. We apply exponential moving average (EMA) to stabilize optimization, with an EMA decay factor of 0.999. We use a cosine noise schedule with 300 diffusion timesteps and adopt the velocity ( v v )-prediction parameterization. The model is trained with a unified objective across all imaging domains and modalities. To incorporate domain-specific physical constraints, we introduce a physics-guided regularization term during diffusion training. The physical loss is activated using a warm-up strategy, starting from epoch 100 and gradually increasing until epoch 150. The base physical loss scale is set to 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} .. This warm-up strategy allows the diffusion model to first learn the general latent distribution before introducing physics-based constraints.
